column1: What is the core invariant governing arcade system design regarding CPU operations and video timing?
column2: Every operation has an opportunity cost measured in scanlines—CPU cycles are shared with video refresh, sound synthesis, and interrupt routines, so time spent on one subsystem directly reduces the budget available for game logic.

column1: Why doesn't a Z80 clocked at 3.58 MHz deliver 3.58 million useful operations per second to game logic?
column2: Because the CPU must share bus access with video refresh circuitry and sound hardware, suffers WAIT-state stalls when video asserts bus steal, and has a 4-cycle minimum instruction latency (11-15 cycles for 16-bit operations).

column1: What are the two 'precious computational windows' in CRT-based arcade hardware, and why are they critical?
column2: Horizontal blanking interval and vertical blanking interval (VBlank)—these are the only safe times to update sprite coordinates, swap palettes, or acknowledge interrupts without causing raster artifacts (torn/corrupted images).

column1: What happens if an NTSC-designed arcade game runs unmodified on PAL hardware, and why?
column2: It gains ~20ms extra per frame (~11 extra scanlines of VBlank) because PAL runs at 50Hz/312 scanlines vs NTSC's 60Hz/262 scanlines, which alters the interrupt budget and can make music run audibly flat.

column1: What problem does tilemapping solve, and how does it work?
column2: It solves the economic problem of expensive DRAM by storing reusable 8x8 pixel patterns (tiles) once in ROM and referencing them via small index values in VRAM, reducing a 256x224 4bpp frame buffer from 28,672 bytes to just 896 bytes for a 32x28 tile screen.

column1: What is the architectural invariant underlying arcade sound and input handling?
column2: Sound generation and input handling must operate independently of the main game loop, governed by hardware interrupts and deterministic timing chains that cannot be preempted by computational load.

column1: How does a Programmable Sound Generator (PSG) like the AY-3-8910 produce tones?
column2: By counting down programmable period registers at a fixed master clock rate and toggling an output bit each time the counter reaches zero, producing a symmetric square wave whose frequency equals the master clock divided by twice the period value.

column1: What is the modulation index (I) in FM synthesis, and what does it control?
column2: I = Δf / f_m (peak frequency deviation divided by modulator frequency); it controls timbral brightness—low indices produce subtle vibrato, while indices above 2 generate complex harmonic/inharmonic overtones.

column1: In FM synthesis, where do output sidebands appear relative to carrier and modulator frequencies?
column2: At f_c ± n·f_m, where f_c is carrier frequency, f_m is modulator frequency, and n ranges over integer multiples determined by the modulation index.

column1: What fundamental physical limitation does bank switching solve in cartridge-based systems?
column2: The finite address bus (e.g., 6502's 16-bit bus = 65,536 bytes max); bank switching uses a mapper chip to intercept writes to trigger addresses and reconfigure which ROM chip or ROM slice the CPU sees at a given address range.

column1: How is a cartridge mapper structurally analogous to a modern OS concept?
column2: It functions like virtual-to-physical address translation via page tables—except the mapper's 'page table' is a handful of flip-flops reconfigured by the program itself through deliberate bus writes, and the CPU never knows a switch occurred.

column1: Why did most golden-age arcade PCBs solder ROMs directly to the motherboard instead of using cartridge slots?
column2: Because operators purchased complete boards (not consumer cartridges), allowing designers to tailor the memory map exactly to the game's data size without needing a standardized mapper interface—at the cost of serviceability (requiring desoldering to swap games).
